description: Solo team building Skydrift, a web tool that blinks NASA SPHEREx infrared images of any patch of sky and flags what moved between survey passes.
summary: Skydrift is a public web tool that shows how any patch of sky changes in NASA's SPHEREx images. Enter an object name or coordinates and it plays the SPHEREx survey passes back like a short film, so anything that moved jumps out. It also subtracts or adds passes, switches between six infrared bands, builds a spectrum for any source you click, and uses a small neural network to flag the sources that moved, with their speed and direction, cross-checked against the Gaia catalog. Skydrift reads SPHEREx images straight from NASA's public cloud bucket with its own index of 1.6 million exposures, so it kept working during the hackathon while the archive's search service was offline. It matters because SPHEREx will image more than a billion objects, and nearby brown dwarfs, fast stars and possibly new planets can only be found by people comparing images over time. Skydrift makes that a one-link task for anyone.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Skydrift takes an object name (resolved through CDS Sesame) or RA and Dec. Names of fast-moving objects are corrected for proper motion so the field is centred where the object is now. It finds every SPHEREx Level 2 exposure covering that position, groups them into survey passes, and stacks each pass into one image.

Blink mode flips between passes. Subtract mode shows each pass minus the first, where a mover appears as a blue and orange pair. Add mode averages all passes for a deeper image. There are six wavelength bands, one per SPHEREx detector, from 0.75 to 5 microns, and the field of view runs from 3.4 to 9.2 arcminutes.

Click any source to get its spectrum: Skydrift measures the source in every individual exposure and plots flux against wavelength, coloured by survey pass.

A mover detector checks every source in the field and lists the ones that shifted, with speed in arcseconds per year and compass direction. Each flagged source is matched to Gaia DR3. A match with the same motion is marked as a known star. A flagged source that Gaia says is still is reported as ruled out. A flagged source that is not in Gaia is marked for a closer look.

The target, band and field of view are in the URL, so any view can be linked or embedded. Images draw as dark stars on a light background by default, like the photographic plates that were blinked to find Pluto, because faint sources are easier to see that way. A night-sky style is one click away.

HOW IT WORKS

Sky index: a script reads the pointing of every SPHEREx Level 2 image from its FITS header in NASA's public bucket, using small byte-range requests. The index covers 1,628,230 exposures from April 2025 to October 2026 and is stored as 4,584 static files, one per sky cell. Adding a new data release is one command.

Cutouts: a SPHEREx image is 65 MB. A small server route reads the header, works out where the wanted pixel rows start, and requests only those bytes. 24 cutouts take about one second.

Stacking, in the browser: each cutout is mapped through its full TAN-SIP distortion solution, resampled north-up at half-pixel steps, background-subtracted and median-stacked per survey pass.

Mover detector: a three-layer convolutional network (about 94,000 weights) takes a 15 by 15 pixel stamp of a source in the first and last pass and outputs the probability that it moved and the shift in pixels. It was trained on 6,740 real SPHEREx star pairs from 400 random fields. For half of the examples the second pass is slid by a known sub-pixel offset, which gives movers with a real point-spread function, real noise and real brightness changes. The network runs in the browser in plain TypeScript.

DOES IT WORK

On 1,351 held-out star pairs the detector catches 95% of slid stars at a 1% false-alarm rate, with a median shift error of 0.7 arcseconds.

On the challenge's test targets: Barnard's Star is measured at 10.1 arcsec/yr north (Gaia: 10.4), Epsilon Indi B at 4.2 arcsec/yr southeast (Gaia: 4.7). RW Aurigae and R Draconis are variable stars and are correctly reported as not moving. WISE 0855-0714, a cold brown dwarf that Gaia cannot see, is flagged at 8.0 arcsec/yr west in the 4.4 to 5.0 micron band and 7.5 arcsec/yr west in the 3.8 to 4.4 micron band (published: 8.1), and is reported as not in Gaia. That is the case the tool is built to surface.

On real moving stars: the detector was run on 140 stars that Gaia measures moving faster than 1 arcsecond per year. 41 of them shifted by at least half a Skydrift pixel between the first and last SPHEREx pass, which is the smallest shift the tool reports. It recovered 31 of those 41 (76%), and its speeds differ from Gaia's by a median of 11%. Of 2,130 other sources in the same fields, 10 were flagged (0.5%), before the Gaia cross-check.

BENEFITS AND GOALS

Volunteers have found most known brown dwarfs by blinking WISE images. Skydrift gives them the same workflow for SPHEREx, with spectra and an automatic first pass on what moved. The current limit is motion of about 1.5 arcseconds per year, set by SPHEREx's 6-arcsecond pixels and 18-month baseline. Every new survey pass lowers that limit.

TOOLS

TypeScript, Next.js, React and Tailwind CSS for the web tool, hosted on Vercel. Python with NumPy, Astropy, SciPy, aiohttp and PyTorch for the sky index, training and validation. Source code: https://github.com/TarunYadgirkar/skydrift
dataRefs: SPHEREx Level 2 spectral images and spectral WCS calibration, DR1 and QR3 (NASA/IPAC IRSA)
IRSA cloud access: public bucket nasa-irsa-spherex
WiseView (Backyard Worlds), model for the blink interaction
projectRefs: ESA Gaia Data Release 3 (ESA Gaia Archive)
Open-source software and fonts: Next.js, React, Tailwind CSS, Phosphor Icons, NumPy, Astropy, SciPy, aiohttp, PyTorch, Bricolage Grotesque, IBM Plex (listed in the README)
Claude (Anthropic), used as a coding and writing assistant
